sentences.text: Paraptenodytes was an extinct genus of penguins belonging to the family Spheniscidae, ranging in size from a Magellanic penguin to an emperor penguin.
The humerus of this animal has rounded ventral and dorsal condyles, unlike the elongated ones found in Arthrodytes, with a total length between 90 and 150 mm.
For many years, a specific specimen described by Simpson was the most complete known fossil penguin skeleton and the only one with an associated skull until Marplesiornis was described in 1960.
George Gaylord Simpson described a new specimen of the type species in 1946, which included associated skull and postcranial parts.
The genus Paraptenodytes was named by Florentino Ameghino in 1891 for fossils originally described by Moreno and Mercerat as Palaeospheniscus antarcticus.
Fossils of Paraptenodytes were discovered in the Santa Cruz and Chubut Provinces of Patagonia, Argentina, coming from the Gaiman, Monte León, and Santa Cruz Formations.
The holotype of Paraptenodytes antarcticus is deposited in the Museo de La Plata in Argentina and comes from the Monte León Formation of the Early Miocene.

A second species, Paraptenodytes robustus, has been described, referred to the San Julián Formation of the Eocene-Oligocene, with its holotype deposited in the Natural History Museum in London, England.

The genus includes the type species P. antarcticus, P. robustus, and the disputed species P. brodkorbi, while former names include Metancylornis, Isotremornis, and Treleudytes, all proposed by Ameghino in 1905.
Paraptenodytes forms the subfamily Paraptenodytinae with Arthrodytes, a group that is not ancestral to modern penguins.
Recent phylogenetic analyses suggest that Paraptenodytes is more closely related to living penguins than to Paleogene giant penguins.
Fossils of Paraptenodytes date from the Early to Middle Miocene, possibly extending into the Pliocene, living from 23.04 to 15.98 million years ago during the Aquitanian to Burdigalian stages.
